What is a Compiler?.code: Frontend vs backend, analysis vs synthesis phases, compilation vs interpretation.

Language Processors.code: Compilers, interpreters, assemblers, transpilers, JIT compilers.

Phases of Compilation: Compilation is organized into front-end (lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis), middle-end (IR generation, optimization), and back-end (instruction selection, register allocation, code emission). This separation enables retargeting and shared optimizations.
What is a Compiler: A compiler translates high-level source code into low-level machine code (binary) executable by hardware. Unlike interpreters that execute code line-by-line, compilers process entire programs before execution. The compilation process involves multiple phases: lexical analysis (tokenization), syntax analysis (parsing), semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, optimization, and final code generation. Compiled languages (C, Rust, Go) generally produce faster executables than interpreted ones (Python, JavaScript) because optimization happens at compile-time. Cross-compilers generate code for different target architectures (e.g., compiling on x86 for ARM). Just-in-Time (JIT) compilers like V8's TurboFan and Java's HotSpot combine compilation with runtime profiling for adaptive optimization. The first compiler was written by Grace Hopper in 1952 (A-0 system), and the first self-hosting compiler (able to compile its own source code) was for Lisp in 1962.
Interpreters vs Compilers: Interpreters execute source code directly without a separate compilation step. They process code statement-by-statement, making them easier to debug (immediate feedback) but slower at runtime due to repeated analysis. Pure interpreters parse and execute each time code runs, while JIT (Just-in-Time) compilers like V8 (JavaScript), HotSpot (Java), and LuaJIT combine both approaches: profiling execution paths and compiling hot code to native machine code at runtime. Trade-offs: compilers have slower startup (compilation time) but faster execution, interpreters have instant startup but slower execution. Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation (e.g., C, Rust, Go) produces standalone executables. Modern language implementations often use multi-tier compilation: fast interpreter → simple JIT → optimizing JIT based on execution frequency. GraalVM (polyglot) and .NET's RyuJIT demonstrate advanced compilation techniques. WebAssembly represents a portable compilation target that runs in a virtual ISA at near-native speed.

Error Handling.code: Error detection, reporting, recovery; panic mode, error productions.

Symbol Tables.code: Symbol table structure, scope management, inserting and looking up symbols.

Abstract Syntax Trees: ASTs represent the essential structure of code, abstracting away syntactic details like parentheses and semicolons. Each node represents a language construct with typed children.
Parsing Fundamentals: Parsing builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) from the token stream. The parser verifies the program follows the language grammar (CFG in BNF notation). Parse errors indicate syntax violations.

Context-Free Grammars.code: Productions, terminals, non-terminals, start symbol; derivation and parse trees.

Top-Down Parsing.code: FIRST and FOLLOW sets, LL(1) grammars, left recursion elimination.

Bottom-Up Parsing.code: LR(0), SLR, LR(1), LALR(1) parsers; shift-reduce and reduce-reduce conflicts.

LL vs LR Parsing: LL parsers (top-down) are simpler and easier to write by hand. LR parsers (bottom-up) can handle more grammars. LALR(1) is used by Yacc/Bison. GLR handles ambiguous grammars.

Error Recovery in Parsing.code: Panic mode, phrase-level recovery, error productions, global correction.

Error Recovery: Panic mode skips to a synchronizing token on error. Phrase-level recovery applies local fixes. Modern compilers produce multiple errors with useful suggestions.

Parser Generators.code: Yacc/Bison, ANTLR; grammar specifications, action code, conflict resolution.

Tokenization Basics: Lexical analysis (tokenization or lexing) is the first compiler phase, converting source code characters into tokens. A lexer reads the input stream and groups characters into lexemes (meaningful sequences) tagged with token types: keywords (if, while, return), identifiers (variable names), literals (numbers, strings), operators (+, -, *), delimiters ({, }, ;), and comments. Lexers use deterministic finite automata (DFAs) to recognize patterns. Regular expressions define token patterns. The lexer discards whitespace and comments. Lexer generators like Lex (flex) and ANTLR produce efficient lexers from declarative specifications. Maximal munch principle: always match the longest possible token. Error recovery in lexers involves skipping bad characters and reporting meaningful diagnostics. Reserved keywords are separate from identifiers: 'if' is a keyword, not a variable. Modern compilers often combine lexing and parsing in a single pass.

Regular Expressions.code: Regular expressions, NFA/DFA conversion, Thompson construction.

Regular Expressions & DFAs: Regular expressions describe token patterns. A DFA recognizes regular languages in O(n) time. Lexer generators like Flex convert regex patterns to efficient DFA-based matchers.

Tokens & Lexemes.exp: Understanding tokens in the compilation process.
Tokens & Lexemes.code: Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, delimiters; token patterns and attributes.

Finite Automata.exp: DFA and NFA for lexical analysis.
Finite Automata.code: Deterministic and non-deterministic finite automata, state transition diagrams.

Lexer Generation.code: Lex/Flex, re2c; specification format, actions, and conflict resolution.

Handwritten Lexers.code: Buffer management, lookahead, sentinel characters, performance optimization.

Lexer Generators: Flex and Lex generate fast DFA-based lexers from regex specifications. Modern alternatives include ANTLR and RE2C. Hand-written lexers are common for simpler languages.

Type Systems.code: Strong vs weak typing, static vs dynamic, subtyping, polymorphism.

Type Checking: Type checking ensures operations are applied to compatible types. It builds a symbol table mapping names to types and scopes. Static typing checks at compile time; dynamic typing defers to runtime.

Attribute Grammars.code: Synthesized attributes, inherited attributes, attribute evaluation, L-attributed grammars.

Type Inference: Hindley-Milner type inference deduces types without annotations via unification. Type variables are assigned to unknown types, constraints are collected and solved to find the most general type.

Scope Resolution.code: Lexical scoping, nested scopes, name hiding, hoisting.

Symbol Tables: Symbol tables map identifiers to their attributes. Scopes are nested; inner scopes can access outer scopes. The most-closely-nested rule governs name resolution.

Control Flow Graphs: A CFG represents all paths through a program. Nodes are basic blocks (straight-line code). Edges represent control flow. Dominance, natural loops, and data-flow analysis use the CFG structure.
Three-Address Code: Three-Address Code (TAC) decomposes expressions into simple operations with at most three operands. Each instruction is a quad (op, arg1, arg2, result). TAC exposes data flow for optimization.
SSA Form: Static Single Assignment (SSA) assigns each variable exactly once. Phi functions merge values at control flow joins. SSA simplifies constant propagation, dead code elimination, and register allocation.

IR Generation.code: Translation schemes, addressing modes, temporary variables.

Function Prologues/Epilogues.code: Caller/callee save registers, stack layout, activation records.

Target Code.code: Instruction selection, addressing modes, machine-specific idioms.

Register Allocation: Graph coloring assigns virtual registers to physical registers. Variables with overlapping live ranges interfere and cannot share a register. Uncolorable variables are spilled to memory.
Instruction Selection: Instruction selection matches IR operations to target instructions. Tree rewriting, maximal munch, and DAG-based selection are common approaches. LLVM uses DAG-based matching.

Lex & Yacc.code: Lex/Flex for lexer generation, Yacc/Bison for parser generation.

LLVM.code: LLVM IR, optimization passes, backend code generation, Clang.

Multi-Stage Compilation.code: Object files, linker, loader, dynamic linking, position-independent code.

Just-In-Time Compilation.code: Hotspot detection, profiling, tiered compilation, dynamic recompilation.

Compiler Testing.code: Test suites, regression testing, fuzzing, differential testing.

Type Systems & Language Design: Type systems range from nominal (Java) to structural (TypeScript, Go). Gradual typing mixes static and dynamic checks. Rust's ownership model uses linear types. Algebraic data types with pattern matching provide safe sum types.
LLVM & Clang: LLVM provides a modular compiler infrastructure: Clang frontend, LLVM IR middle-end, and target-specific backends. Rust, Swift, and Julia use LLVM. MLIR extends LLVM for domain-specific compilers.
Parser Generators: Yacc and Bison generate LALR(1) parsers from grammar specifications. ANTLR generates LL(*) parsers. Tree-sitter provides incremental parsing for IDEs.

Register Allocation.code: Graph coloring, liveness analysis, interference graphs, spilling.

Instruction Scheduling.code: Pipeline hazards, instruction latencies, list scheduling, software pipelining.

Local Optimizations.code: Common subexpression elimination, constant folding, algebraic simplification.

Global Optimizations.code: Data-flow analysis, reaching definitions, live variable analysis.

Loop Optimizations.code: Loop invariant code motion, induction variable elimination, loop unrolling.

Constant Folding: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time. x = 2 * 3 becomes x = 6. Constant propagation replaces variables that are always constant with their values.
Dead Code Elimination: DCE removes instructions whose results are never used. In SSA form, trace back from output-producing instructions and mark everything else as dead.
Loop Optimizations: Key loop optimizations: invariant code motion, induction variable strength reduction, loop unrolling, fusion, fission, and vectorization. Loops are the primary optimization target.
